items.readable_text:
Content:
When a real-world object is shaped like a rectangular prism, we use the volume formula:

Content:
[MATH: V = \text{length} \times \text{width} \times \text{height}.]

Content:
If there are several identical objects, first find the volume of one object. Then multiply by the number of objects.

Content:
For example, suppose a storage box is [MATH: \dfrac{5}{2}\,\textrm{ft}] long, [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\,\textrm{ft}] wide, and [MATH: 3\,\textrm{ft}] high. Let's find the total volume of [MATH: 3] identical boxes.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/48e85ffc0f02f0e2dfc2fc26ea886908]

Content:
First, find the volume of one box:

Content:
[MATH: V|= (5)/(2) × (2)/(3) × 3; = (5 × 2 × 3)/(2 × 3 × 1); = (30)/(6); = 5.]

Content:
So, one box has a volume of [MATH: 5\,\textrm{ft}^3.]

Content:
Since there are [MATH: 3] boxes,

Content:
[MATH: 3 \times 5 = 15.]

Content:
The total volume of the boxes is [MATH: 15\,\textrm{ft}^3.] Remember to include cubic units when giving a volume.

To solve these problems:

Be sure the units match. Volume is measured in cubic units (such as [MATH: \text{ft}^3] or [MATH: \text{in}^3]), and the rate is given "per cubic unit."

Content:
For example, suppose a block of soap is shaped like a rectangular prism that is [MATH: 2\,\textrm{in}] long, [MATH: \dfrac{3}{2}\,\textrm{in}] wide, and [MATH: \dfrac{4}{3}\,\textrm{in}] high, and each cubic inch of soap costs [MATH: \[math]4.]

Content:
[MATH: V|= 2 × (3)/(2) × (4)/(3); = (2 × 3 × 4)/(1 × 2 × 3); = (24)/(6); = 4]

Content:
So, the block has a volume of [MATH: 4\,\text{in}^3.] Since each cubic inch costs [MATH: \[/math]4,] we get

Content:
[MATH: 4 \times \[math]4 = \[/math]16.]

Content:
Therefore, the total cost of the soap block is [MATH: \[math]16.] Always find the volume first, then multiply by the unit cost.

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
When a real-world object is shaped like a rectangular prism, we use the volume formula:

Content:
[MATH: V = \text{length} \times \text{width} \times \text{height}.]

Content:
If there are several identical objects, first find the volume of one object. Then multiply by the number of objects.

Content:
For example, suppose a storage box is [MATH: \dfrac{5}{2}\,\textrm{ft}] long, [MATH: \dfrac{2}{3}\,\textrm{ft}] wide, and [MATH: 3\,\textrm{ft}] high. Let's find the total volume of [MATH: 3] identical boxes.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/48e85ffc0f02f0e2dfc2fc26ea886908]

Content:
First, find the volume of one box:

Content:
[MATH: V|= (5)/(2) × (2)/(3) × 3; = (5 × 2 × 3)/(2 × 3 × 1); = (30)/(6); = 5.]

Content:
So, one box has a volume of [MATH: 5\,\textrm{ft}^3.]

Content:
Since there are [MATH: 3] boxes,

Content:
[MATH: 3 \times 5 = 15.]

Content:
The total volume of the boxes is [MATH: 15\,\textrm{ft}^3.] Remember to include cubic units when giving a volume.

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we make a drawing of the tank.

[IMG: /graphics/10d5948bd646cdd3e768397c206daec7]

The volume of the tank is:

[MATH: V|= length × width × height; = 2 × (4)/(3) × (3)/(2); = (2)/(1) × (4)/(3) × (3)/(2); = (2 × 4 × 3)/(1 × 3 × 2); = (24)/(6); = 4]

Therefore, the tank will be able to store [MATH: 4 \, \textrm{m}^3] of water.

Item 5 — Tutorial: Unit Costs for Volumes

Content:
Sometimes we need to find the total cost of a rectangular prism when we know the cost per cubic unit.

Content:
To solve these problems:

Content:
1. Find the volume.
2. Multiply the volume by the cost per cubic unit.

Content:
Be sure the units match. Volume is measured in cubic units (such as [MATH: \text{ft}^3] or [MATH: \text{in}^3]), and the rate is given "per cubic unit."

Content:
For example, suppose a block of soap is shaped like a rectangular prism that is [MATH: 2\,\textrm{in}] long, [MATH: \dfrac{3}{2}\,\textrm{in}] wide, and [MATH: \dfrac{4}{3}\,\textrm{in}] high, and each cubic inch of soap costs [MATH: \[math]4.]

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/bbbd3d32d06c710ef792b6766cbfbb22]

Content:
To find the cost of the soap block, we first find the volume:

Content:
[MATH: V|= 2 × (3)/(2) × (4)/(3); = (2 × 3 × 4)/(1 × 2 × 3); = (24)/(6); = 4]

Content:
So, the block has a volume of [MATH: 4\,\text{in}^3.] Since each cubic inch costs [MATH: \[/math]4,] we get

Content:
[MATH: 4 \times \[math]4 = \[/math]16.]

Content:
Therefore, the total cost of the soap block is [MATH: \[math]16.] Always find the volume first, then multiply by the unit cost.
